claims.text: The initial material is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial coating contains dislocation networks and stacking faults at 300 K.
Above 900 K, rapid thermal activation initiates stacking-fault annihilation.
Stacking-fault annihilation is followed immediately by the onset of amorphization.
Thermal energy above 900 K exceeds the stacking-fault energy barrier.
Stacking-fault annihilation and lattice disordering form an amorphous interfacial layer.
Dislocation starvation produces a transition from crystalline plasticity to localized amorphization.
Amorphization eliminates the dislocation-mediated plasticity barrier.
The resulting amorphous interfacial layer has low shear strength.
The amorphous interfacial layer facilitates rapid wear.
Formation of the amorphous layer causes a sharp increase in the coefficient of friction.
Formation of the amorphous layer causes a precipitous drop in wear resistance.
Pure thermal dislocation glide would instead produce gradual softening.
At 600 K, dislocation density decreases while crystalline order is maintained.
The reduction in dislocation density at 600 K results in increased elastic modulus.
A significant decrease in HCP atom count together with near-zero dislocation line length would indicate amorphization rather than mechanical annealing.
If friction and wear degradation occur after pre-annealing while HCP atom count remains high, stacking-fault annihilation is not required for the proposed amorphization mechanism.

contradictions.description: The amorphous layer is described as low-friction and low-shear-strength, yet its formation is also claimed to cause a sharp increase in the coefficient of friction. No additional mechanism reconciles the claimed low-friction interface with the friction spike.
